newsitem.title: USA: Chubais says Russian economy to surprise the world.
newsitem.headline: Chubais says Russian economy to surprise the world.

text.p: Russia's reform chief Anatoly Chubais, delighted with new loans from the World Bank and a 1997 policy agreement with the IMF, said on Tuesday that Russian economic growth could surprise the world next year.

Chubais told a news conference that Russia had signed a protocol for a $600 million World Bank loan and agreed 1997 economic policy priorities with the International Monetary Fund during the semi-annual meetings of the organisations.
He predicted a modest rise of between 0.5 percent and 2.5 percent in Russian gross domestic product this year, but said things could get better fast.
"I do not think 1997 will be the year for huge growth in Russia, but if you look to 1998, I think that is a year when you could be surprised," Chubais, a First Deputy Prime Minister, said.
Russian economic output has declined stubbornly in the five years since Moscow launched its first reform programme in 1992, although officials say the worst is over.

The IMF, which expects to restart disbursements on a stalled $10 billion three-year loan next month, sees three percent GDP growth this year, but Washington officials decline to predict Russia's performance in 1998.
"There are too many variables," an international monetary official said.

He said Russia's statement on economic policy for 1997, signed by Central Bank chairman Sergei Dubinin on Tuesday, would force Moscow to meet ambitious targets on revenue collection and structural reforms.
"The 1997 programme is very ambitious on the revenue side and even if they achieve that, the expenditures they can finance are very low. But that is the only way they can survive," he said.
"If they fail on the revenue side and cannot finance these expenditures, then they are really in very deep trouble, politically and socially. They will not be able to pay wages and pensions."
Wage and pension arrears are already a major problem for the government, which is drawing up plans for drastic spending cuts to bring the IMF loan programme back on track.
The 1997 policy statement has not been made public, but officials say it also outlines detailed targets on structural reform and monetary policy.
"They have shown over the last two years that they have handled monetary policy well and we are confident that this will be okay," the monetary official said.

Russian annual inflation fell to 21.8 percent last year, from 131 percent in 1995 and Chubais, who said inflation was "completely under control", said inflation would not be more than 12 percent in 1997.
Russian officials see the IMF agreement as a way to ease their access to Eurobond markets and to guarantee Moscow a significant place in the world community.

Russia is also looking for speedy membership of the World Trade Organisation and it wants to join the Paris Club of creditor states, viewing membership as a way to get back some of the funds lent by Moscow to its Soviet-era allies.

Chubais said the officials with whom he talked during the IMF meetings had made clear that President Boris Yeltsin would have a full role at the next big meeting of world leaders, the summit of the seven leading industrialised nations in Denver.
"Denver will not be G7 or G7+1," he said. "It will be a meeting of the Eight in which the Russian president will take part on a full-scale basis."
